nodes.label: AMPM Platform — The Questions Still Open (round two, R1 to R19)
nodes.rationale: Second, shorter round of client questions dated 26 October 2026, after AMPM answered all twenty-five original questions on 25 October. Compiled from three sources so nothing is asked twice: the eleven items AMPM's own brief lists under 'Items to confirm before development', the two points raised by the developer, and the open points recorded in the decision log while applying the 25 October answers (several of which were on nobody's list). Written so each point can be decided in a minute or two: each question states what is needed, why it matters, what AMPM's documents already say (quoted), what the developer proposes, and the choices. Nine questions need a real decision (R1, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8, R11, R17); for the other ten a tick on the drafted proposal is enough. Answers go into the decision log beside the 25 October answers, the drafts move to version 0.3, and the milestone schedule and cost estimate are then drafted.

nodes.label: Group 1: Getting in — the demo, payment and refunds
nodes.rationale: Groups the three commercial-entry questions (R1 demo limits, R2 gateway, R3 refunds) because they all gate the moment a prospect becomes a paying subscriber and all have lead times outside the code: demo data preparation, a merchant account in AMPM's name, and refund wording on the payment screen.

nodes.label: Group 2: The client side
nodes.rationale: Groups R4 to R8: what clients can reach (browser as well as apps), who they are (one shared login or two accounts), how a decision is completed (one approval or both), what money they see, and which hotel services carry a fee. These five decide the client-facing surface and therefore the largest open cost item in the estimate.

nodes.label: Group 3: Your team (roles, cost visibility, staff sign-in)
nodes.rationale: Groups R9 and R10 because both are about internal access: every screen, permission and test in the drafts is built on the staff role list, and staff accounts reach costs and identity documents, so they need stronger authentication than a client account.

nodes.label: Group 4: Guests (RSVP link structure)
nodes.rationale: Holds the single guest-facing open point (R11): the link style decides the first screen of the RSVP form, how duplicates are prevented, and which drafted tests run.

nodes.label: Group 5: Privacy and retention
nodes.rationale: Holds R12. AMPM's Q8 and Q17 answers both point at one decision — retention periods plus privacy wording — which is why AMPM's item 9 and the developer's Q8 and Q17 are treated as the same question.

nodes.label: Group 6: Technology and operations — we propose, you approve
nodes.rationale: Groups R13 to R17, the points AMPM's documents leave to be approved with the developer rather than decided alone: hosting and recovery, capacity, messaging providers, service levels, and the go-live shape. Framed as proposals to approve because the brief says AMPM will approve these arrangements with the development team before launch.

nodes.label: Group 7: Changes and the end of a wedding
nodes.rationale: Groups R18 and R19: the two workflow rules at the end of a project's life — when a change counts as material and who approves it, and who approves archiving and how access is restored later. Both are rules inside flows that are already built, so only the named approver and the threshold values are missing.

nodes.label: Short answers and defaults to tick
nodes.rationale: Eight small defaults that a tick keeps and a line changes: accounting-software export for Finance (CSV by default, since the platform issues no GST invoices); privacy-respecting analytics on public pages plus a bot check on enquiry and demo forms; who at AMPM signs each phase's acceptance on staging; emergency reading of identity documents by the Super Admin, audited each time; RSVP reminder cadence then a call from the RSVP team, with no guest edits after the deadline; readiness checklists hidden from the client; programme and calendar files for guests once invitations go out; one subscription per client account rather than per wedding.

nodes.label: Where each question came from, and the repeats (R to Q and draft traceability)
nodes.rationale: Maps every R question to AMPM's eleven brief items, the developer's Q number, the draft sections that also ask it, and whether AMPM's own documents already answer it — so the same question is never asked twice. Records the merges: AMPM items 1 and 2 are one question (R1), item 9 covers Q8 and Q17 (R12), and item 3 is half answered by the brief's own section 3. R3, R4, R6, R7, R8, R10, R11, R16 and R17 were on no AMPM list; they come from the business explanation, the specification or the decision log. Also notes that the drafts' review sections still list questions the 25 October answers settled, which will be removed at the next revision.

nodes.label: Answer sheet (R1 to R19)
nodes.rationale: One-line-per-question table so AMPM can reply by number instead of reading the prose. Returned answers are recorded in the decision log next to the 25 October answers, the drafts move to version 0.3, and the milestone schedule and cost estimate are drafted — those last two waiting on R4, R14 and R17 in particular.

nodes.label: R1: Demo duration, locations and hotels per location (real or invented)
nodes.rationale: The demo is the first thing a prospect sees and the only trial offered. Its limits are settings, so changing them later costs nothing, but the demo data must be prepared before launch and whether the hotels are real or invented decides who prepares it: invented samples need six hotel pages written and photographed from scratch. Proposal: seven days from first OTP sign-in, extendable once by Sales; three locations (already applied); two hotels per location; real hotels flagged demo-visible with indicative price ranges and masked rate details, so the demo looks like the product and Eva's data does the work. AMBIGUITY: the brief says 'up to two sample hotels' while its closing note records that AMPM's notes mention both one hotel per city and two; duration is mentioned nowhere in AMPM's documents.

nodes.label: R2: Payment gateway provider for the Rs 50,000 subscription
nodes.rationale: Only the provider is open: the brief's section 3 already settles the transaction-handling requirements (payment record; amount, date, status and transaction reference; activation after confirmation; no duplicate activation from repeated notifications; start and expiry dates; staff review of payment status) and all of it is in the drafts. The merchant account takes one to two weeks to open and must be in AMPM's name, and the gateway code is written in Phase 1. Proposal: Razorpay with hosted checkout and activation driven by the gateway's notification, unless AMPM already has a merchant account elsewhere; PayU and Cashfree fit the same adapter, so a swap is a few days of work as long as card, UPI and payment notifications are supported.

nodes.label: R3: Subscription cancellation and refund rule
nodes.rationale: On no list until now: AMPM's business explanation section 9 lists cancellation and refund terms as still to be confirmed, rule 8 says refund terms must be confirmed before implementation, and the 25 October answers are silent. The portal has to say something at the moment of payment and Finance needs a button or a rule. Proposal: no refund once the subscription is activated, because access is immediate and the data stays with the client; full refund if AMPM cancels before activation or cannot deliver; refunds made by Finance through the gateway and recorded against the payment. A cooling-off rule adds a check at refund time; case-by-case adds a Finance permission and a recorded reason. A refund path through the gateway is designed (finding GP-7) but no refund wording is in the drafts.

nodes.label: R4: Client portals in the browser as well as in the apps
nodes.rationale: Raised by the developer, not on AMPM's list, and the largest open cost item. Families compare hotels with photographs, menus and price grids, which many prefer on a laptop; the demo is reached from the website; app-only means every prospect installs an app before seeing the demo. Against that, a web version is a further build to design, test and maintain. Both AMPM documents can be true at once: the original specification asked for a responsive desktop, tablet and mobile interface, while the brief asks for iOS and Android and leaves the final architecture to be agreed. Proposal: option B, the discovery and wedding portals also run in the browser, built from the same code as the client app so screens are designed once; the team app stays native because of offline wedding-day use. Option C removes the client app and its app-store work; option A is cheapest but costs the laptop experience and adds an install step before the demo.

nodes.label: R5: Two representative accounts or one shared login
nodes.rationale: CONFLICT between AMPM's two documents of 25 October: the compiled questions and answers say under Q5 that both representatives will use the same login credentials, while the brief's section 5 says the choice must be finalised before development and that separate authenticated accounts are preferable for security and audit history. The brief's position is the later and more considered one and matches the developer's recommendation. With one shared login the system cannot tell who approved a design, menu or budget line — the audit trail says only 'the client' — and one phone number has to receive both families' OTPs. Proposal: two accounts with identical rights on the same wedding; they still share responsibility, they just do not share a phone.

nodes.label: R6: Does one representative's approval complete a decision, or must both approve
nodes.rationale: The specification's section 13 lists whether multiple approvals are required among the decisions to confirm, and the 25 October answers settle who is authorised but not how many. One approval keeps things moving; two protect both families on money matters but add a step to every approval screen plus a wait whenever one representative is unavailable. Proposal: one approval for everything in the first release, with the number as a setting per approval type so budgets and contracts can later require two while designs and menus require one. Two approvals add a 'waiting for the other side' state and a reminder to the second representative.

nodes.label: R7: Which amounts the client sees in the wedding portal
nodes.rationale: Raised by the developer. AMPM's rule on what must never be shown is clear (internal costs, margins, vendor rates, quotations, negotiations); what is shown is not, yet both the business explanation and the specification ask for a client-facing budget and the specification lists financial visibility among the decisions to confirm, so those screens cannot be signed off. Since milestone payments are not collected online in the first release, the amounts are shown for information only. Three levels: level 1 planned budget and approved amounts per function; level 2 adds invoices issued to the client and payment status; level 3 adds actual spend and variance per line. The drafts currently show level 3; the proposal is level 2, keeping actual spend and variance internal. Level 1 removes the invoices and payments screens from the client portal for now. Separately, hotel booking-milestone amounts are assumed visible only where the client pays the hotel directly.

nodes.label: R8: Which hotel services carry a fee beyond the subscription
nodes.rationale: The business explanation's section 9 lists fees for hotel research, negotiation, site visits and booking assistance among the decisions the developer must not assume, and the 25 October answers do not return to it. The answer decides whether a client can request a site visit with one tap or whether the request first produces a service agreement to accept; the amounts themselves stay outside the app, like the wedding management fee. Proposal: keep the assumption — availability checks included in the subscription, and negotiation, site visits, contract review and booking assistance behind an accepted service agreement with the fee recorded on it, even when that fee is zero for a particular client. 'All included' removes the agreement step from the hotel flow; 'everything by agreement' moves it earlier, before the first availability check.

nodes.label: R9: Staff roles, and who may see hotel costs and vendor costs
nodes.rationale: Every screen, permission and test in the drafts is built on the role list, so it has to be final: the brief names departments only as functional examples and says the final list must follow AMPM's approved staff structure, while cost visibility is the one permission the brief singles out as restricted to specifically authorised personnel. Assumed nine roles from the specification: Super Admin; Sales / Relationship Manager; Hotel / Destination Team; Wedding Project Manager; Creative / Design Team; Vendor Coordinator; RSVP / Guest Team; Hospitality / Logistics Team; Finance / Accounts. Hotel costs visible to Super Admin, Finance and the Hotel Team; vendor costs to Super Admin, Finance and the Vendor Coordinator; the Project Manager sees both for their own weddings; everyone else sees client-facing amounts only. Adding or renaming a role is a day of work; moving cost visibility is a permission change plus a test change. Open sub-point: whether 'senior authorised management' needs a role of its own or is the Super Admin role.

nodes.label: R10: How staff sign in
nodes.rationale: Clients sign in by mobile number and OTP, as decided, but the brief's section 13 defers the staff method to the development team. Staff accounts reach costs, identity documents and every wedding they are assigned to, so they need stronger protection, and staff work inside venues with poor signal where an SMS code may not arrive. Proposal: email, password and a six-digit authenticator-app code, which works without network on the wedding day. Alternatives: password plus SMS OTP, which makes the SMS provider a wedding-day dependency for the team app; or sign-in through Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 if AMPM uses one, which gives central control when someone leaves but needs the workspace account details.

nodes.label: R11: RSVP link structure — per side, combined, or household links
nodes.rationale: The brief requires separate bride's-side and groom's-side links and allows one combined link where AMPM chooses to use it; the compiled answers say the final link structure is to be decided. The choice decides the first screen of the RSVP form, how duplicates are prevented, and which drafted tests run: with per-side or combined links a guest must find themselves in the loaded list before responding, while a private link per household removes that step but needs a phone number or email for every household up front. Proposal: per-side links as the standard and the combined link as a per-wedding option, both in the first release since they share one mechanism, keeping household links available for weddings whose list arrives with contacts.

nodes.label: R12: Retention periods and privacy wording
nodes.rationale: AMPM's answers say nothing is deleted automatically and that AMPM approves retention and deletion, so the system needs the periods after which it proposes a deletion for approval, and the enquiry and RSVP forms need agreed privacy notices before launch. AMPM's Q8 and Q17 answers point at this one decision, which is why AMPM's item 9 and the developer's Q8 and Q17 are merged here. Assumed periods: closed leads 24 months; guest personal data 12 months after the wedding project closes; identity documents 30 days after checkout; demo data reset on a schedule. When a period ends the system lists the records and a Super Admin approves — nothing is deleted unattended — and notices are designed to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023. Periods are settings; wording supplied by AMPM instead of drafted by the developer shortens Phase 3 by a few days.

nodes.label: R13: Hosting, backups, recovery and account ownership
nodes.rationale: Hosting decides where personal data lives, how fast the platform is for users in India, what a disaster costs, and who owns the infrastructure if the development relationship ends; the specification lists technology ownership among the decisions to confirm and nothing in AMPM's documents decides it, so this is a proposal to approve. Assumed: AWS Mumbai with backup copies in Hyderabad so all personal data stays in India; database recoverable to any point in the last 35 days plus daily snapshots in the second region; files versioned and copied across regions; at most 15 minutes of data lost and the platform back within 4 hours, with a restore rehearsed quarterly; accounts, domains and provider accounts in AMPM's name with the development team as delegated administrators; the full production set-up built from Phase 1 rather than a throwaway. The same design runs on Google Cloud or Azure Indian regions — a change of names in the plan — while tighter recovery targets need a warm standby at roughly double the database cost.

nodes.label: R14: Capacity — staff, weddings, guests, hotels and media
nodes.rationale: The numbers size the database, the storage and the load tests, and they go into the cost estimate. AMPM's answer gives two of the four — about 200 hotels and about 20 concurrent weddings — while the brief asks that staff and guest capacity be confirmed before implementation; the business explanation's worked example is a 250-guest wedding in Jaipur. The drafts were originally sized for 50 staff, 40 concurrent weddings, 1,500 guests per wedding, 500 hotels and 2 TB of media in the first year, and are now rescaled to 200 hotels and 20 weddings with staff and guests unchanged. Proposal: confirm 50 staff accounts and 1,500 guests as upper bounds. Larger numbers change indexing and the storage estimate, not the design.

nodes.label: R15: WhatsApp, SMS and email providers and account ownership
nodes.rationale: WhatsApp Business onboarding and Indian SMS registration (DLT) take two to six weeks and must be done in AMPM's name, so they start before coding; because clients sign in by OTP, the SMS provider is a launch dependency. The brief proposes email, WhatsApp and SMS as channels with provider selection to be confirmed. Assumed: WhatsApp through the WhatsApp Business Platform via an Indian business solution provider, email through Amazon SES, SMS through a DLT-registered Indian provider for OTP and as a fallback, all three behind one adapter so a later swap is contained. Proposal: the developer selects the business solution provider and the SMS provider on price and reliability while AMPM owns the accounts, and AMPM creates its Meta Business Manager and registers the sender for DLT in the first week. Deferring WhatsApp removes the longest lead time but leaves only email and SMS at launch.

nodes.label: R16: Service levels, support and wedding-day on-call
nodes.rationale: New point, proposed in the architecture draft and never addressed: the brief asks for reliable backups and recovery and the specification lists maintenance and support responsibility, but no document names an availability target or says who answers the phone during a wedding. These targets drive the maintenance contract and part of the running cost. Assumed: 99.5 percent availability per month excluding announced maintenance; most requests under 0.4 seconds; portal pages usable within 3 seconds on 4G; WCAG 2.1 AA for the client and guest portals; the last two versions of the major browsers; development-team on-call on wedding days and no deployments while any wedding is live. Office-hours support lowers maintenance cost but leaves wedding-day incidents to AMPM staff until the next working day; a higher availability target changes the hosting design and its cost.

nodes.label: R17: One go-live, or hotel discovery first
nodes.rationale: Raised by the developer and the decision that shapes the schedule more than any other open point, which is why the schedule and cost estimate wait on it. Hotel discovery is the product sold by subscription and is complete at the end of Phase 1, while the wedding modules take three more phases: launching discovery first brings subscriptions in months earlier and lets real prospects test the demo, at the price of two go-lives and support starting earlier. AMPM's documents give the first release's content but never say whether it is one date or two. The drafts currently gate one launch at the end of Phase 4 with discovery-first noted as the open alternative. Proposal: option B, discovery live at the end of Phase 1 and the wedding modules as one second go-live, so the first wedding managed in the system is one whose discovery happened in it. B and C add a stabilisation pass and a support window per go-live; A delays the first subscription to the end of Phase 4.

nodes.label: R18: Material-change thresholds and who approves a material change
nodes.rationale: Material changes trigger review tasks and notifications, so too low a threshold floods the team and too high a one lets a large change through unnoticed; the thresholds are configurable as AMPM asked but need starting values, and the approval rule is a workflow to build. AMPM's Q25 answer says the definition is not finalised and that budget-change percentages, date and venue thresholds will be decided by AMPM. Assumed: material when a budget line moves 10 percent or more, or a function's date or venue changes, raising impact flags and review tasks for the affected teams, with the client's approval following the normal approval rule (R6). Proposal adds 5 percent of the total approved budget, and a second approver — Super Admin or senior management — above roughly 15 percent of the total budget. Values are settings; a second approver adds a step and a waiting state to the change-request flow.

nodes.label: R19: Archiving a wedding and restoring access later
nodes.rationale: DECIDED in substance: the brief's section 11 already sets read-only client access for three months after the wedding, then archiving on AMPM's approval, with records not automatically deleted, later access controlled by AMPM, and archiving defined as a change of status and permissions rather than deletion. Only the mechanics are missing, because the three-month window and the archive are built but the approval step and the reopening path need a named person and a rule. Assumed: a reminder to the representatives before the window ends; the Project Manager proposes archiving and the Super Admin approves; client memberships are removed so the representatives can still sign in and see a contact route but no project; archived weddings stay readable to authorised staff and are excluded from day-to-day lists. Proposal adds the reopening rule: a representative asks AMPM, the Super Admin restores read-only access for 30 days with a logged reason, editing never reopens, and later corrections are made by staff with a note. All of these are rules inside one flow; none changes the data.
